text:
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

Hundal v. Border Carrier Ltd.,

2011 BCSC 1703

Date:
20111026

Docket:
S089125

Registry: Vancouver

Between:

Najam
Hundal

Plaintiff

And

Border
Carrier Ltd., Sukhdev Singh Bains, and

Royal City Trucking Ltd.

Defendants

And

Karachi
Transport Ltd.

Defendant by Counterclaim

Before: The Honourable Madam Justice Fenlon

Oral Reasons for Judgment

Counsel for the Plaintiff:

A.
Aguilar

Counsel for the Defendants and Defendant
by Counterclaim:

P.K.
Shergill

Place and Date of Trial:

Vancouver,
B.C.

October 11-14, 17-21, 24-26, 2011

Place and Date of Judgment:

Vancouver,
B.C.

October 26, 2011

[
1
]

THE COURT:
On
the first day of trial, the defendants applied to strike out those portions of
the plaintiff’s pleading claiming oppression, conflict of interest, conspiracy
and unjust enrichment. I will simply refer to all four claims as the oppression
claim, because the underpinning of the application for all of the claims is
that the wrongs alleged are really wrongs done to the company and not to the
plaintiff personally and therefore cannot be maintained by him.

[
2
]

I dismissed the application with reasons to
follow. These are my reasons for that decision.

[
3
]

Rule 9-5(1)(a) of the
Supreme Court Civil
Rules
provides:

(1)  At any stage of a proceeding, the court
may order to be struck out or amended the whole or any part of a pleading,
petition or other document on the ground that

(a) it discloses
no reasonable claim or defence, as the case may be

…

and the court
may pronounce judgment or order the proceeding to be stayed or dismissed and
may order the costs of the application to be paid as special costs.

[
4
]

The principles to be applied in determining
whether a reasonable claim is alleged are as follows:

1.

No evidence is to be considered, only the
pleadings: Rule 9-5(2).

2.

The facts alleged are to be taken as proven:
Canadian
Bar Assn. v. British Columbia
(2008),
2008 BCCA 92 (CanLII)
, 76 B.C.L.R. (4th) 48 (C.A.) at
para.
37
.

3.

The notice of claim must be read as generously
as possible so as to accommodate any inadequacies in the form of the
allegations which are merely the result of drafting deficiencies:
Evergreen
Building Ltd. v. IBI Leaseholds Ltd.
,
2005 BCSC 1929
at para.
2
.

4.

A pleading should not be struck if it could be
amended to disclose a reasonable claim:
Horton Bay Holdings Ltd. v. Wilks

(1991), 3 C.P.C. (3d) 112 at p. 119
.

5.

It must be plain and obvious that no reasonable
cause of action is disclosed. If there is a chance that the plaintiff might
succeed, then he should not be driven from the judgment seat:
Odhavji Estate
v. Woodhouse
(2003),
2003 SCC 69 (CanLII)
, 233 D.L.R. (4th) 193 (S.C.C.) at para.
15
.

6.

The weakness of the case is no reason to strike.
The sole question is whether the plaintiff presents a question fit to be tried:

Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v. Canadian Jewish Congress
(1999),

1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
, 36 C.P.C. (4th) 266 (B.C.S.C.) at para.
37
.

[
5
]

It is apparent from this review that the bar is
set quite high for the applicant. Counsel for the defendants submits that the
plaintiff’s claim in oppression does not disclose a reasonable cause of action
because Mr. Hundal is claiming in his personal capacity for wrongs done to
the defendant corporation, Border Carrier Ltd.

[
6
]

Under the rule in
Foss v. Harbottle

(1843), 67 E.R. 189 (Ch.)
, the company and its shareholders are different legal
entities. It follows that only the company can sue for harm done to it. The
proper way for a shareholder to proceed in such a case is by bringing a
derivative action on behalf of the company.

[
7
]

In contrast, an oppression claim is a personal
claim made by a shareholder. It arises only when a shareholder has suffered
direct harm, a harm that must be more than simply a loss of share value
consequent upon a harm caused to the company.

[
8
]

Counsel for the defendants submits that none of
the harms pleaded in the statement of claim gives rise to the requisite harm to
Mr. Hundal in his personal capacity.

[
9
]

Ms. Shergill acknowledges that the same
conduct or events giving rise to harm to the company can also give rise to
personal harm to the shareholder, but she argues that, in order to do so, the
conduct must involve a breach of fiduciary duty or other legal obligation owed
to the shareholder by the defendant.

[
10
]

The plaintiff, says Ms. Shergill, has
neither established such a legal obligation nor pleaded how he has been
uniquely affected by the harms to the company alleged to have been committed by
the defendant. She argues that it is not enough to simply describe the harm to
the company and, in the words of Mr. Justice Mackenzie in
Rogers v. Bank
of Montreal
(1984),
1985 CanLII 150 (BC SC)
, 64 B.C.L.R. 63 (S.C.) [
Rogers
] (at
para.
84
), “[hitch] to that allegation” an intention to injure the
plaintiff.

[
11
]

I agree that a bald assertion of harm or a “me
too” pleading is not enough to establish a basis for an oppression claim. The
real character or substance of the plaintiff’s claim must be examined to
determine whether the shareholder has a distinct harm sufficient to ground a
claim in oppression.

[
12
]

In
Rogers
, the Court held at p. 81:

For a
shareholder to obtain a personal right of action there must be relations
between him and the tort-feasor independent of those which the shareholder
derives through his interest in the corporate assets and business.

[
13
]

In assessing the relationship between the
shareholder and the tortfeasor, in this case between Mr. Hundal and
Mr. Bains, many cases have used the language of reasonable expectations.
These expectations may arise from a contract or from a fiduciary duty, as
Ms. Shergill correctly argued, but they are not limited to those
categories.

[
14
]

In
BCE Inc. v. 1976 Debentureholders,

2008 SCC 69 (CanLII)
, [2008] 3 S.C.R. 560, the Supreme Court of Canada said that the oppression
remedy is designed to protect the reasonable expectations of corporate
stakeholders:

[62]      As denoted by “reasonable”, the
concept of reasonable expectations is objective and contextual. The actual
expectation of a particular stakeholder is not conclusive. In the context of
whether it would be “just and equitable” to grant a remedy, the question is
whether the expectation is reasonable having regard to the facts of the
specific case, the relationships at issue, and the entire context, including
the fact that there may be conflicting claims and expectations.

[63]      Particular
circumstances give rise to particular expectations. Stakeholders enter into
relationships, with and within corporations, on the basis of understandings and
expectations, upon which they are entitled to rely, provided they are
reasonable in the context: see
820099 Ontario; Main v. Delcan Group Inc.

(1999),
1999 CanLII 14946 (ON SC)
, 47 B.L.R. (2d) 200 (Ont. S.C.J.). These expectations are what the
remedy of oppression seeks to uphold.

[
15
]

In
Malata Group (HK) Ltd. v. Jung
,
2008
ONCA 111
, the Ontario Court of Appeal recognized that there may be overlap
between derivative and oppression claims:

[30]      ... [T]here is a degree of overlap
between the claims that could be made out as derivative actions and those that
could fall under the oppression remedy. As this court said at para. 5 of
the endorsement, “[t]he two are not mutually exclusive.

[31]      One situation in which the overlap
between the oppression remedy and the derivative action can be found is where
directors in closely held corporations engage in self-dealing to the detriment
of the corporation and other shareholders or creditors. A relevant case in this
respect is
C.I. Covington Fund Inc. v. White
,
2000 CanLII 22676 (ON SC)
, [2000] O.J. No. 4589
(S.C.J.), in which Swinton J. observed at para. 41:

A number of oppression cases turn on the
fact that there has been conduct by directors or majority shareholders that
amounts to self-dealing at the expense of the corporation or other corporate
stakeholders. (
SCI Systems Inc. v. Gornitzki Thompson & Little Co.

(1997), 36 B.L.R. (2d) 207
(Ont. Ct. (Gen. Div.)), aff'd (1998),
1998 CanLII 17741 (ON CTGDDC)
, 110 O.A.C. 160
(Div. Ct.));
Neri v. Finch Hardware
(1976) Ltd. (1995),
1995 CanLII 7412 (ON CTGD)
, 20 B.L.R. (2d)
216 (Ont. Ct. (Gen. Div.));
Loveridge Holdings Ltd. v. King-Pin Ltd.

(1991), 5 B.L.R. (2d) 195
(Ont. Ct. (Gen. Div.)). For example, in
SCI
,
there was oppression because the directors unfairly removed assets from the
corporation so as to prevent the payment of a corporate debt and to benefit
themselves.

[
16
]

In
Runnalls v. Regent Holdings Ltd.
,
2010
BCSC 1106
a recent case of this Court, Mr. Justice N. Smith noted at
para. 44:

Where an
alleged wrong is to the company, the usual remedy is a derivative action under
s. 232 of the
Business Corporations Act
, rather than an oppression
claim by individual shareholders. However, in a closely held corporation with a
small number of shareholders, the same conduct may give rise to either or both
remedies because conduct that results in a loss to the company may also have a
direct impact on shareholders in their individual capacities...

[
17
]

A particularly relevant case in the same vein is

Gopal v. Burke
,
2007 BCSC 1930
, a decision of Master Young dealing with
an application to amend a petition to include a claim that the respondent
diverted corporate opportunities from the company in which the plaintiff was a
shareholder. Master Young said at para. 15:

... [T]he
diversion of corporate opportunities is derivative, but if the opportunities
are diverted to a majority shareholder of the company (the miscreant so to
speak), then the wrong impacts a minority in a disparate manner and this assumes
a personal flavour.

[
18
]

In the case before me a two-person company is in
issue and the plaintiff claims that corporate opportunities were diverted from
one of the two 50% shareholders (and I emphasize I am not making any findings
as to whether those claims have been made out in this ruling, I am simply
considering whether the claim as it is described can stand in law and lead to a
trial). It is alleged that one shareholder in this case obtained a significant
benefit, either directly, or indirectly through the company he controls, while
the other shareholder did not receive that benefit. What is alleged is not
simply that Border Carrier Ltd. has suffered a loss, but that the loss has
resulted in a sufficiently disparate impact on the two shareholders, Mr. Hundal
and Mr. Bains, that the injury has a personal impact on one of them, in
this case the plaintiff.

[
19
]

I agree with Ms. Shergill that the
plaintiff’s pleading in this case is deficient because it does not expressly
plead that the plaintiff had a reasonable expectation that the defendants would
not engage in each of the acts set out in paras. 7(a) through (n) of the
pleading, nor does it plead expressly the existence of a duty or an agreement
between the two shareholders that decisions would not be made about the
company’s affairs except by mutual consent, although that is arguably an
allegation implicit in the statement of claim. Finally, the basis for the
oppression claim should have been better supported in the pleading. The
plaintiff should have expressly, rather than implicitly, stated that the
defendant shareholder through his company benefited by the conduct complained
of while the plaintiff did not, therefore resulting in a disparate impact on
the plaintiff.

[
20
]

As I noted in giving my decision on the first
day of trial, this is not an application that was brought frivolously. I have
considered it carefully, and I have given fairly extensive oral reasons on an
interim ruling for that reason.

[
21
]

As I noted at the outset of these reasons, a
pleading should not be struck if it may be amended to disclose a reasonable
claim. In my view these pleadings, while they are deficient, could readily be
amended to remedy the deficiencies. Furthermore, doing so, even on the first
day of trial, does not prejudice the defendants because the facts relied on by
the plaintiff and the harm alleged are and have been clearly defined and have
been thoroughly canvassed on examination for discovery and through production
of documents.

[
22
]

Accordingly, I have concluded that it is not
plain and obvious from the pleadings that the plaintiff cannot succeed in a
claim for oppression and the other remedies in issue and the defendants’
application must therefore be dismissed.

The Honourable Madam Justice L.A. Fenlon
